units.label: Verbal n-back base（主容量曲线）
units.description: 以字母流执行1、2、3-back；ChatGPT逐试次判断当前字母是否与n步前相同，形成工作记忆容量的主要比较轴。

units.label: Verbal n-back 操作变体
units.description: 在 verbal base 上分别加入噪声、逐试次反馈和要求逐步推理，用于观察干扰与提示策略如何改变容量表现。

units.label: Spatial n-back base
units.description: 用ASCII 3×3网格中的X位置替代字母刺激，执行1、2、3-back，保持match/nonmatch输出结构。

units.label: Spatial n-back 操作变体
units.description: 在空间任务上复用噪声、反馈和CoT/逐步推理变体，考察干扰、反馈与提示对空间工作记忆表现的影响。

units.label: Abstract spatial reasoning variants
units.description: 将match规则改为与n步前位置同一行和/或同一列，并区分是否排除相同位置，以增加空间关系判断要求。

units.label: Spatial grid-size comparison
units.description: 比较3×3、4×4、5×5和7×7网格，考察可用空间位置数和跨试次干扰的关系。

units.label: Cross-model verbal-base comparison
units.description: 在verbal base上比较GPT-3.5、GPT-4及六个其他模型，观察容量曲线是否跨模型重复。

units.label: 共享的逐试次记录、计分与统计分析
units.description: 各实验共享逐trial的match/nonmatch目标、模型反应、正确性和反应时间记录，并以hit rate、false alarm rate、accuracy和d′汇总，再比较n-back水平。

facts.statement: 作者把问题表述为测量ChatGPT的工作记忆容量，并比较verbal与spatial n-back在不同条件下的容量限制；论文还将n-back表现与人类行为研究中的工作记忆测量联系起来。

method_function.text: 以LLM完成认知任务并观察负荷、干扰和策略条件下的行为轨迹。

facts.statement: 正式分析单元包括ChatGPT的verbal/spatial任务及其变体，以及verbal base上的跨模型比较；同一n-back序列中的单个trial是重复测量记录，不单独视为实验。

method_function.text: 将共享序列、不同模型和操作变体分开，同时保留共享计分流程。

facts.statement: verbal base使用字母表bcdfghjklnpqrstvwxyz，按n=1、2、3构造字母序列；每个block有24个字母，8个match和16个nonmatch。

method_function.text: 提供可控制n-back负荷的离散字母刺激与目标标签。

facts.statement: 论文称模型通过OpenAI API逐试次完成任务，主要模型为gpt-3.5-turbo、temperature=1，其余参数默认；每个条件的n=1、2、3各生成50个block。

method_function.text: 把模型调用单位和任务负荷明确绑定到逐trial程序。

facts.statement: verbal变体分别加入每试次3–6个噪声符号、上一试次正确/错误反馈，或要求模型逐步思考并给出理由。

method_function.text: 分别操纵干扰、反馈和外显推理提示。

facts.statement: spatial base用ASCII 3×3网格表示位置，以X标记九个位置之一；每个block有24个grid，8个match和16个nonmatch。

method_function.text: 将空间位置编码为可输入语言模型的离散文本刺激。

facts.statement: 空间实验包括noise、feedback、CoT变体；另有两种abstract spatial reasoning规则，以及3×3、4×4、5×5、7×7网格大小比较。

method_function.text: 通过改变空间关系判定规则和可用位置数分解任务难度与干扰。

facts.statement: match trial要求模型输出m，nonmatch trial要求输出-；每个trial记录stimulus、target、response、correct和response time。

method_function.text: 把模型输出转成二元行为反应并保留trial级正确性与时间。

facts.statement: verbal代码先随机抽取match位置，match时复制n步前刺激；nonmatch分支只在i>n时排除与n步前相同的字母。因此首个可比较位置i=n若落入nonmatch分支，可能出现字母相同却标成nonmatch；前n个位置也标为nonmatch。空间抽象2代码按同行/同列且不相同的规则生成，并额外排除与上一刺激相同的nonmatch。未见固定随机种子；以上是静态实现事实，不证明出版数据中实际发生错标。

method_function.text: 构造目标/非目标序列并避免把非目标误生成目标。

facts.statement: 作者代码在每个block内持续追加user stimulus和assistant response到messages，因此同一block的后续trial在累积对话上下文中执行；block间重新建立messages。

method_function.text: 保持block内历史上下文，形成连续的逐试次任务。

facts.statement: verbal base代码先接受严格m或-，否则取首字符，仍非法就抛错。所查CoT代码在首字符非法时追加纠错提示并再次请求模型，循环到首字符为m或-；该循环未见显式次数上限。首字符有效时，后续历史追加的是提取后的m/-，不能假设原始完整推理文本一直保留。代码未执行，实际重试次数和结果影响未知。

method_function.text: 将可能带有解释文本的反应压缩为可计分的m/-类别。

facts.statement: 汇总指标包括hit rate、false alarm rate、accuracy和d′。代码先在每个block计数并计算指标，将hit/false-alarm比例裁剪到0.01–0.99后算绝对值d′；随后在同一n水平的blocks之间取均值和np.std(...)/sqrt(blocks)作为标准误。不是在单个block内对d′求标准误。

method_function.text: 同时保留信号检测指标和准确率，减少极端比例对正态反变换的影响。

facts.statement: 作者把d′约等于1设为容量阈值：某个n水平的d′降到约1时，定义模型的工作记忆容量在该n附近受限。

method_function.text: 把连续的检测敏感性轨迹转为作者定义的容量界限。

facts.statement: 统计代码对不同n的d′使用Kruskal–Wallis检验、两两Mann–Whitney U检验及Bonferroni校正，并计算epsilon-squared和rank-biserial correlation；另以单侧Wilcoxon检验d′是否高于1。

method_function.text: 比较负荷水平和容量阈值，不把总体准确率作为唯一结果。

facts.statement: 论文报告verbal表现随n从1升到3显著下降；除noise变体外，其他三个verbal变体的d′在n=3约降到1，加入noise会进一步降低容量。

method_function.text: 提供负荷和干扰对工作记忆表现的行为轨迹。

facts.statement: 论文报告空间任务总体比verbal更困难，CoT能提高空间表现；abstract spatial reasoning变体的容量更低。

method_function.text: 比较刺激类型和空间关系规则对容量曲线的影响。

facts.statement: 更大网格显示更高d′；作者提出可能因为跨trial刺激干扰减少，但明确把这一解释留给未来研究，并提出在人类任务中检验其可推广性。

method_function.text: 区分观察到的网格效应和作者尚未验证的机制解释。

facts.statement: verbal base跨模型比较显示GPT-4表现高于其他模型；作者没有用GPT-4测试n>3，因此不能由该实验确定GPT-4的精确容量上限。

method_function.text: 保留模型比较的结果范围与上限不确定性。

facts.statement: README记录的是30 blocks、每block 30 trials、10 match/20 nonmatch，而论文正文和实验代码记录50 blocks、24 trials、8 match/16 nonmatch；两版不能静默合并。

method_function.text: 后续引用必须区分仓库旧说明和论文/实验实现，不能把README数字当作主实验参数。

facts.statement: 分析代码在跨模型比较段把blocks改为30并注释为缩短时间；这与主实验使用50 blocks不同。

method_function.text: 跨模型结果的聚合样本量和主实验不能直接视为同一分析设置。

facts.statement: 静态检查代码未见固定随机种子或序列版本清单；因此不能声称仅凭仓库即可重建论文使用的随机序列。

method_function.text: 限制序列层面的精确重建与重复试验比较。

facts.statement: 代码使用d′=abs(norm.ppf(hit)-norm.ppf(false_alarm))，绝对值会隐藏hit rate低于false alarm rate时的方向；这是实现层面的计分限制。

method_function.text: 后续解释d′时需保留方向信息缺失这一实现事实。

facts.statement: 逐trial调用在block内累积messages，使后续试次输入包含先前刺激和记录的模型响应；论文未把这种上下文累积单独操纵或量化其影响。它是解释n-back表现时需要保留的实现边界，不能由此断言n越大上下文必然越长。

evidence.quote: paper, we systematically assess the working memory capacity of ChatGPT, a large language model developed by OpenAI, by examining its performance in verbal and spatial n-back tasks under various conditions. Our experiments reveal that ChatGPT has a working memory capacity limit strikingly similar to that of humans. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of different instruction strategies on ChatGPT’s performance and observe that the fundamental patterns of a capacity limit persist. From our empirical findings, we propose that n-back tasks may serve as tools for benchmarking the working

We devised two categories of n-back tasks involving verbal and spatial working memory (Szmalec et al. 2011) respectively and prompted ChatGPT (using the OpenAI API, model = “gpt-3.5-turbo”, temperature = 1, other parameters are set to default values) to complete the tasks in a trial-by-trial manner. For both categories, we have a base version task and several variants derived from the base version further to test the model’s performance under different conditions. To compare the performance of ChatGPT with other LLMs, we also used API of the following LLMs to perform the base version of the verbal task: {Bloomz-7B, Bloomz-7B1-mt, ChatGLM-6B v1.0, ChatGLM-6B v1.1, GPT-4, Vicuna-7B, Vicuna-13B}. Verbal n-back experiments. In the base version of the verbal n-back task (see Figure 3a), for n = {1, 2, 3}, respectively, we generated 50 blocks of letter sequences using an alphabet commonly found in the literature (“bcdfghjklnpqrstvwxyz”). Each block contained a sequence of 24 letters, which are presented one at a time as user input to the API. We included 8 match trials and 16 nonmatch trials in each block. The LLM was instructed to respond with “m” on match trials and “-” on nonmatch trials.

Figure 3: Illustrations of the variants of verbal n-back tasks (also applicable to spatial tasks). We use n = 2 in the figure. (a): base version identical to the case presented in Figure 1 (top row); (b): stimulus on each trial now contains 3-6 random noise characters (chosen from “#$%&@ˆ˜”) in addition to a single alphabetical letter that the LLM should compare across trials. The LLM is instructed to ignore these noise characters, and the alphabetical letter may appear in any position in the noise-corrupted stimulus; (c): alongside the input for every trial, the LLM is also provided with feedback on whether it has performed the previous trial correctly; (d): the LLM is prompted with a reasoning-eliciting instruction to output the final answer (“m” or “-”) and the rationale. Refer to Table 1 for the detailed prompts. Apart from the above base version, we further explored the behavioral performance of ChatGPT on the following three variants of the task: • We added 3 to 6 noise symbols to the input on every trial to examine the LLM’s behavior when it is impossible to get the correct answer by simply doing a string match between stimulus inputs (see Figure 3b). • In human behavioral studies, a common strategy to improve participants’ performance is to provide feedback after each trial (Shalchy et al. 2020). Here in the variant, after the LLM gave a response for the current trial, we provided feedback on whether its response was correct or wrong alongside the stimulus input of the following trial (see Figure 3c). • Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting has proved helpful in eliciting reasoning in LLMs (Wei et al. 2022c). In this variant, we instructed the LLM to think step by step when giving a response (see Figure 3b).

For n = {1, 2, 3}, respectively, we generated 50 blocks of grid sequences, each grid featuring a letter X in one of the nine positions. Note that the letter X was arbitrarily chosen to represent an occupied spatial location textually and could be substituted by any other letter or symbol. Each block contains 24 grids, including 8 match trials and 16 nonmatch trials. Like in the verbal n-back tasks, the LLM was instructed to respond with “m” on match trials and “-” on nonmatch trials. We further explored the spatial working memory capacity of ChatGPT with the following modifications of the task: • Similar to the variants of verbal n-back tasks, we also had “spatial-with-noise”, “spatial-with-feedback”, and “spatial-with-CoT-reasoning” versions of the task. The with-feedback and with-CoT-reasoning variants were basically the same as those for the corresponding verbal tasks. For the spatial-with-noise version, we added a noise character (chosen from “#$%&@ˆ˜”) to 1 to 3 unoccupied locations in the 3 × 3 grid on every trial, so that we could

• To test if the LLM can reason in a more sophisticated way, we further introduced two variants that specifically require abstract spatial reasoning. For the first variant (see Figure 4c), a match is defined as when the location of the letter X is in the same row and/or column (i.e., including identical locations) as the X n trials ago. For a second variant (see Figure 4d), a match is defined as when the letter X appears in the same row or column, but not both (i.e., excluding identical locations). This constraint would further force the LLM to use abstract reasoning and instruction-following abilities to perform this task. Given the increased difficulty of these two variants, we expect the LLM would have a worse performance on these two variants compared to other variants. • We also explored whether the size of the grid (3 × 3, 4 × 4, 5 × 5 or 7 × 7) would influence the LLM’s performance (see Figure 4b). To the best of our knowledge, there have not been human studies exploring how the number of all possible spatial locations would impact behavioral performance in spatial n-back tasks. In light of this, we did not have specific assumptions for how the LLM would perform differently under these scenarios.

To analyze the model’s performance in our experiments, we used four widely accepted performance metrics reported in numerous human behavioral studies: hit rate, false alarm rate, accuracy and detection sensitivity.  In the current study, we did 50 blocks of tests for n = {1, 2, 3} in each experiment, which allows us to calculate the standard error of the mean (SEM) and draw error bars to visualize the reliability of our findings. Among the four metrics, the pattern of hit rates and false alarm rates can vary a lot depending on the specific task condition (Chooi and Logie 2020). Accuracy, in turn, will also be biased by very high/low hit rates and false alarm rates. In contrast, detection sensitivity(d′ ) is a much more robust performance metric. A higher d′ indicates better performance, suggesting that the individual is more accurately distinguishing between targets and non-targets. Based on the overall difficulty of the current task, we set d′ = 1 as the threshold to determine the working memory capacity of a model: if, at a certain level of n, the model’s d′ drops to around 1, we can define that its working memory capacity is limited to n. Verbal n-back experiments. In the verbal task variants, we observed a performance pattern strikingly consistent with human participants, with the LLM’s performance declining significantly when n increased from 1 to 3 (Figure 5). Furthermore, apart from the noise variant, all of the other three variants have a working memory capacity of around 3: their d′ drops to around 1 when n = 3. Adding noise significantly reduces the model’s working memory capacity, which is analogous to distracting stimuli presented in human working memory experiments (Gaspar et al. 2016). To investigate whether other LLMs exhibit similar performance patterns, we tested 7 other LLMs on the base version of the verbal n-back task (Figure 9). Strikingly, GPT-4, which is arguably the most intelligent LLM today, also possesses a working memory capacity that  10053  far exceeds that of other LLMs. However, due to the high cost of calling the API of GPT-4, we did not test it with n > 3 to determine its exact working memory capacity. This consistent pattern thus might be reflecting a fundamental constraint that emerged from the architecture of the model, suggesting a possibility that the low-level mechanisms of working memory in ChatGPT might be similar to human working memory, at least in some aspects. Our model comparison results further confirm that the performance of LLMs on n-back tasks can be a reliable metric for assessing their working memory capacity, which in  10054  turn might reflect the general intelligence of reasoning and problem-solving emerged from these models. Here we created a dataset to test the working memory capacity of language models. We choose the N-back task because it is widely used in cognitive science as a measure of working memory capacity. To create the N-back task dataset, we generated 30 blocks of trials for $N = \{1, 2, 3\}$, respectively. Each block contains 30 trials, including 10 match trials and 20 nonmatch trials. The dataset for each block is stored in a text file. The first line in the text file is the letter presented on every trial. The second line is the condition corresponding to every letter in the first line ('m':this is a match trial; '-': this is a nonmatch trial). We have created many versions of the N-back task, including verbal ones and spatial ones.  **Prompt Example.** Here we only focus on the base version of verbal N-back tasks. We use the following format of prompts for $N = \{1, 2, 3\}$:

def compute_summary_stats(all_trials, exp_name, n_list, blocks):     summary_stats = {}     raw_data = {}     for n in n_list:         hit_rate, false_alarm_rate, accuracy, response_time, d_prime = [], [], [], [], []         for b in range(blocks):             trials = all_trials[f"{n}back_{b}"]              # Compute the hit rate, false alarm rate, and response time             hits, false_alarms, total_targets, total_lures, total_rt = 0, 0, 0, 0, 0             for trial in trials:                 if trial['target'] == 'm':                     total_targets += 1                     if trial['correct']:                         hits += 1                         total_rt += trial['rt']                     elif trial['correct'] == '':                         raise ValueError("Missing data in " + exp_name + " " + str(n) + "-back task, block " + str(b) + '.')                 else:                     total_lures += 1                     if trial['correct'] == '':                         raise ValueError("Missing data in " + exp_name + " " + str(n) + "-back task, block " + str(b) + '.')                     elif not trial['correct']:                         false_alarms += 1              hit_rate.append((hits / total_targets) * 100)             false_alarm_rate.append((false_alarms / total_lures) * 100)             accuracy.append(((hits + total_lures - false_alarms) / (total_targets + total_lures)) * 100)             response_time.append(total_rt / hits if hits > 0 else np.nan)              # Compute d prime             hit_rate_adjusted = np.clip(hits / total_targets, 0.01, 0.99)             false_alarm_rate_adjusted = np.clip(false_alarms / total_lures, 0.01, 0.99)             d_prime.append(np.abs(norm.ppf(hit_rate_adjusted) - norm.ppf(false_alarm_rate_adjusted)))

def nonparametric_test(raw_data, n_list):     metrics = ["d_prime"]     U_list = []     corrected_p_list = []     r_list = []     for metric in metrics:         # print(f"Kruskal-Wallis test for {metric}:")          # Prepare the data for Kruskal-Wallis test         data = [np.array(raw_data[n][metric]) for n in n_list]          # Perform Kruskal-Wallis test         H, p = kruskal(*data)          # Calculate degrees of freedom         df = len(n_list) - 1          # Calculate the total number of observations         N = len(raw_data[n_list[0]][metric]) * len(n_list)                  # Calculate epsilon squared (ε²):ε² = (H - k + 1) / (N - k), where H is the Kruskal-Wallis H statistic, k is the number of groups (in your case, len(n_list)), N is the total number of observations across all groups         epsilon_squared = (H - len(n_list) + 1) / (N - len(n_list))          # print(f"  H({df}) = {H:.4f}, p = {p:.4f}, epsilon squared = {epsilon_squared:.4f}")          # Perform post-hoc Mann-Whitney U test         # print("  Post-hoc Mann-Whitney U test:")         for combo in itertools.combinations(n_list, 2):             n1, n2 = combo             data1 = raw_data[n1][metric]             data2 = raw_data[n2][metric]              # Mann-Whitney U test             U, p_value = mannwhitneyu(data1, data2)              # Bonferroni correction             corrected_p = min(p_value * len(list(itertools.combinations(n_list, 2))), 1)              # Calculate the effect size using the rank-biserial correlation (r): r = 1 – (2U)/ (n1 * n2)             r = 1 - (2 * U) / (len(data1) * len(data2))             U_list.append(U)             corrected_p_list.append(corrected_p)             r_list.append(r)             # print(f"    {n1}-back vs {n2}-back: U = {U:.4f}, p = {corrected_p:.4f}, rank-biserial correlation(r) = {r:.4f}")         # return (H, p, epsilon_squared) and (U_list, corrected_p_list, r_list)         return (H, p, epsilon_squared), (U_list, corrected_p_list, r_list)

# define a function to test for each n in n_list if the d' is significantly larger than 1 def test_dprime(raw_data,n_list):     stats_list = []     p_list = []     r_list = []     data = [np.array(raw_data[n]["d_prime"]) for n in n_list]     for n in range(len(n_list)):         # Subtract the hypothesized median (1 in this case) from the data         differences = data[n] - 1         # Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test         statistic, p_value = stats.wilcoxon(differences, alternative="greater")         # Compute the sum of positive ranks and the sum of negative ranks         positive_ranks = np.sum(np.where(differences > 0, stats.rankdata(np.abs(differences)), 0))         negative_ranks = np.sum(np.where(differences < 0, stats.rankdata(np.abs(differences)), 0))         # Calculate the rank-biserial correlation         rank_biserial = (positive_ranks - negative_ranks) / (positive_ranks + negative_ranks)         stats_list.append(statistic)         p_list.append(p_value)         r_list.append(rank_biserial)     return (stats_list, p_list, r_list)
